sourceBindings.text: In this scenario, a junior agronomy technician advises a farmer about Plot C by collecting a composite sample and measuring pH and texture. Treat these as three observed skill chains, not as a quick page-completion exercise. pH and texture inform a preliminary recommendation, but cannot establish the whole soil health or guarantee a successful season. The crop/report reasoning continues in the separate S3-17 step.

The task allocates 25 minutes for practical and 20 minutes for a report, yet its pH method requires air-dried preparation and a 30–60-minute slurry wait. Use documented Stage A collection/label; Stage B own sample preparation and drying; Stage C calibrated pH; Stage D ribbon/feel; Stage E report. Record each stage's start/finish, actual active minutes and waiting separately. A jar or slurry prepared early for teaching may show a waiting effect but never stands in for the student's own sample. The trainer identifies the real pH meter, buffers, sampling purpose, field and laboratory method before practice.

sourceBindings.text: The task allocates 45 minutes work and no discussion: 25 practical plus 20 report writing. Drying and the example’s 30–60-minute equilibration make documented stages necessary. Preserve every personal action and the later one-page report, two crops and at least one management recommendation. The required tools are a planning list, not confirmed availability.

pH and texture provide limited evidence. Soil-health assessment uses multiple physical, chemical and biological indicators; no single pair of results establishes overall excellent soil condition or guarantees a crop season.

sourceBindings.text: Define a reasonably homogeneous management unit and the intended laboratory test. Use a clean suitable probe or spade, a clean plastic bucket, bags and permanent label. The sampling example uses a zigzag/W route, 10–15 subsamples and 6–8 inches (about 15–20 cm) for topsoil. These are example figures, not universal sampling rules; the trainer declares count, depth and excluded atypical areas for Plot C and the actual laboratory. Cover the area, avoid old gateways, fence lines or livestock concentration unless those conditions are the separate question, and record each point and depth.

sourceBindings.text: Break up and mix your own cores thoroughly in the clean bucket, remove stones, roots and large debris as the selected protocol permits, then take a representative portion. The example offers 'about 2 cups or 500 grams'; these are different units. Record an actual mass if 500 g is required, or an actual volume if the lab requests cups; never claim equality without weighing. Label the container immediately with a unique ID, learner, date/time, plot, depth, test purpose and stage; keep the ID with every aliquot and log hand-offs.

sourceBindings.text: For this lesson’s routine dry-soil pH example, the learner spreads a traceable aliquot for appropriate air drying, gently breaks aggregates and passes it through a 2 mm sieve when the chosen method calls for it. The trainer records actual start and end, container, contamination protection and who performed every action. A specimen from a different learner or a ready display tube may help discussion but cannot be assessed as this learner's work. Other analyses may require a different preservation method; do not universally air-dry or refrigerate every soil sample.

Separate the portion used for digital pH from that used for the moist feel test while retaining the parent sample ID. Do not force a 25-minute clock to erase real drying or equilibration. If a sample or meter is unavailable, mark that practical action pending rather than inventing a reading.

sourceBindings.text: The worked example mixes 20 g prepared soil with 20 mL distilled water, a 1:1 **mass:volume** example. It says stir for 30 seconds and equilibrate for 30–60 minutes. A laboratory that says 1:1 **volume:volume** may use a different scoop and wait; the two procedures cannot be blended silently. Before measuring, the trainer selects one written SOP for the actual instrument and intended result, including aliquot basis, water quality, stirring, equilibration, calibration, cleaning and recording. The pH 4, 7 and 10 solutions in this example are buffer examples; use the number and range specified by the actual device/SOP, documenting lot/date and success.

sourceBindings.text: For practical evidence, the eligible learner personally performs the calibration required by the identified meter/SOP under trainer observation, then rinses the probe without contaminating buffers, stirs and places the electrode as instructed, immerses the sensing bulb appropriately, waits for stability and records the actual raw value, sample ID, time, instrument resolution and temperature when relevant. Explaining calibration on an inert or conceptual model is useful preparation but cannot replace this actual calibrated-meter performance. One decimal place is this example’s display format, not permission to invent precision. Digital pH measurement uses a calibrated electrode in a soil suspension, with separate buffer solutions for calibration. Reagent drops in a test tube and comparison with a colour card belong to a colour-reagent method. The two methods use different equipment and procedures; a colour comparison does not demonstrate a digital-electrode measurement.

sourceBindings.text: The feel-test example starts with about 25 g, wets it slowly and kneads it to a moist-putty consistency; this is a useful teaching amount, not an exact required mass. If too dry, add water; if too wet, add dry soil. Squeeze for a ball. Sand may not hold one when moisture is correctly adjusted, which is an observation rather than automatic failure. If a ball forms, press a uniform ribbon between thumb and forefinger, allow it to break under its own weight, and record the length. The inch-based example’s rough branches are no ribbon, under 1 inch, 1–2 inches and over 2 inches. Exactly 1 inch is 2.54 cm and 2 inches is 5.08 cm; the inch-based example’s cutoffs are not exact 2.5/5 cm cutoffs. For a separately declared NRCS-centimetre exercise, use weak under 2.5 cm, medium from 2.5 cm to below 5 cm, and strong at least 5 cm. This assigns exactly 5 cm to the chart's '5 cm or longer' strong branch; it is an explicit tie convention for the chart's overlapping medium/strong wording, not an exact conversion of the inch-based example.

sourceBindings.text: Use the USDA-NRCS texture-by-feel guide after correcting moisture. If the soil still cannot form a ball, the guide leads to sand. If a ball forms but no ribbon forms, it leads to loamy sand, which is different from sandy loam. For a weak ribbon, very gritty wet-rub feel leads to sandy loam; very smooth feel leads to silt loam; if neither predominates, loam. For a medium ribbon, those same three feel branches lead respectively to sandy clay loam, silty clay loam and clay loam. For a strong ribbon, they lead respectively to sandy clay, silty clay and clay. Use the declared length convention, not feel or length alone. Record ball/ribbon behaviour, length, actual feel, class and uncertainty. This field estimate is not quantitative laboratory particle-size analysis.

The feel key has eleven endpoints. The quantitative texture triangle has twelve classes, including silt, which is not a separate endpoint of this first-page key. Feel does not determine particle percentages. Cemented clay aggregates in arid/desert soils can feel like sand or silt; uncertain or conflicting estimates need local reference samples, experienced review or laboratory confirmation.

sourceBindings.text: The trainer checks safe method, accuracy, raw data, sample continuity and explanation for each criterion, marking competent or not yet competent with an observed reason. The example of good sample preparation but faulty meter calibration means only the affected skill needs targeted feedback and practice, followed by a new observed attempt. Preserve both attempts. After reassessment, record the actual observed result, which could still be not yet competent.

The learner's self-assessment item 5.1 can help identify where practice is needed but cannot sign off sampling, pH or texture. The trainer's individual dated evidence and signature are required. If the pH model/SOP or physical site remains unknown, the corresponding skill stays pending. S3-17 uses these results to write a preliminary report, explicitly limited to measured properties and other known context.
